seo.title: HTS Chapter 20: Preparations of Vegetables, Fruit & Nuts — Tariff Rates & Import Duties | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 285 HTS Chapter 20 lines — orange juice, French fries, canned tomatoes, olives, pickles, jams, peanut butter, canned fruit and juices. General, FTA and Column 2 rates plus the 2026 Section 301 duties by country.

overview.intro:
Chapter 20 covers fruit, vegetables and nuts once they have been processed: pickles, canned tomatoes, preserved mushrooms, frozen French fries, olives, jams, canned fruit, peanut butter and fruit and vegetable juices. Its **285 tariff lines** carry a base rate on 264 of them, and the rates come in many forms — 7.85¢ per liter on frozen orange juice, 12.5% on canned tomatoes, 10.1¢/kg (drained weight) on canned pitted black olives, 131.8% on peanut butter imported over its quota.

The U.S. imported **$15.96B** of these goods in 2025. Canada and Mexico supplied 32%, and USMCA-qualifying goods from both enter free. Goods from elsewhere pay the base rate **plus an extra duty by country**: since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff on 60 economies — 10% in total for most EU goods, +10% or +12.5% for most others, +37.5% for Brazil and up to +37.5% for China (see Rates by country). **29 lines are exempt** from that duty for every country, among them orange juice, canned pineapple, mango and papaya products, coconut and palm hearts. Some products — preserved mushrooms, Spanish ripe olives, lemon juice — also face antidumping duties, which the rates here do not include.

productGroups.label: Pickles & vegetables in vinegar
productGroups.blurb: Anything preserved in vinegar: cucumbers and gherkins at 9.6%, capers 8%, artichokes 10.2%, and a long tail of pickled vegetables, fruit and nuts. Mangoes in vinegar (1.5¢/kg) are on the Section 301 exemption list.

productGroups.label: Tomatoes, prepared or preserved
productGroups.blurb: Canned and preserved tomatoes: whole or in pieces at 12.5%, paste, purée and other tomato products at 11.6%. Both are above the 10% EU floor, so EU tomatoes pay the base rate only.

productGroups.label: Mushrooms & truffles, preserved
productGroups.blurb: Preserved mushrooms pay 6¢/kg (drained weight) + 8.5%; truffles are free. Agaricus mushrooms (2003.10) from Chile, China, France, India, Indonesia, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain also face antidumping orders.

productGroups.label: Frozen prepared vegetables, incl. French fries
productGroups.blurb: Vegetables prepared and then frozen. Almost all of the value is frozen potato products such as French fries (2004.10.80, 8%); other frozen vegetable mixes are 11.2%.

productGroups.label: Other preserved vegetables & olives (not frozen)
productGroups.blurb: Shelf-stable vegetables that are not frozen and not in vinegar: olives (per-kg rates on drained weight), beans, sweet corn, peppers, artichokes, sauerkraut and more. Bamboo shoots are free.

productGroups.label: Fruit & peel preserved by sugar (candied, glacé)
productGroups.blurb: Fruit, nuts and peel preserved by sugar — glacé cherries, candied peel, crystallized ginger. Small in trade; pineapple (2.1%) is on the Section 301 exemption list.

productGroups.label: Jams, jellies, marmalades & fruit purées
productGroups.blurb: Jams, jellies, marmalades and fruit purées made by cooking. Most jams are 1.4%–7%; apple, strawberry and papaya pastes and purées are 12%–14%. Pineapple jam and guava and mango purées are exempt from Section 301.

productGroups.label: Prepared fruit & nuts, incl. peanut butter & canned fruit
productGroups.blurb: The largest group: canned and otherwise prepared fruit and nuts — peanut butter, roasted nuts, canned peaches and pineapple, mandarin segments, berry and açaí preparations. Rates run from free to 131.8% on peanut butter over its quota.

productGroups.label: Fruit & vegetable juices
productGroups.blurb: Fruit and vegetable juices, charged mostly per liter of single-strength juice: 7.85¢ on frozen orange juice concentrate, 4.5¢ on not-from-concentrate orange juice; apple juice is free. Orange, lime and some pineapple juice are exempt from Section 301.

rateTable.note: Rates shown in grey are inherited from the parent heading. HTSUS states a duty once on the 8-digit line and leaves the 10-digit statistical lines blank; this table resolves each line to the rate that actually applies to it.

workedExamples.title: A container of frozen French fries from Canada
workedExamples.body: The general rate is 8%. Canada claims USMCA (SPI **S**), which is Free, and USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt from the Section 301 duty (9903.05.93). On $60,000 of fries the duty is **$0**. Fries that do not qualify would pay 8% + 10% (9903.05.29) = **$10,800**.

workedExamples.title: 1,000,000 liters of frozen orange juice concentrate from Brazil
workedExamples.body: The rate is 7.85¢ per liter of reconstituted (single-strength) juice, so concentrate is counted at the volume it makes once water is added (additional U.S. notes 1–2): 1,000,000 × $0.0785 = **$78,500**. Orange juice is on the exemption lists of both Section 301 actions on Brazil (U.S. note 50(a)(ii) and note 52(b)), so no extra duty is added.

workedExamples.title: $100,000 of canned tomatoes from Italy
workedExamples.body: The base rate is 12.5%. For EU goods the Section 301 action sets a 10% total only where the base rate is lower (9903.05.39); 12.5% is higher, so nothing is added: **$12,500**. Tomato paste (2002.90.80, 11.6%) works the same way.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover: (a) vegetables, fruit or nuts prepared or preserved by the processes specified in chapter 7, 8 or 11; (b) vegetable fats and oils (chapter 15); (c) food preparations containing more than 20 percent by weight of sausage, meat, meat offal, blood, insects, fish or crustaceans, molluscs or other aquatic invertebrates, or any combination thereof (chapter 16); (d) bakers' wares and other products of heading 1905; or (e) homogenized composite food preparations of heading 2104.

**Note 2.** Headings 2007 and 2008 do not apply to fruit jellies, fruit pastes, sugar-coated almonds or the like in the form of sugar confectionery (heading 1704) or chocolate confectionery (heading 1806).

**Note 3.** Headings 2001, 2004 and 2005 cover only those products of chapter 7 or of heading 1105 or 1106 (other than flour, meal and powder of the products of chapter 8) which have been prepared or preserved by processes other than those referred to in note 1(a).

**Note 4.** Tomato juice the dry weight content of which is 7 percent or more is to be classified in heading 2002.

**Note 5.** For heading 2007, "obtained by cooking" means obtained by heat treatment at atmospheric pressure or under reduced pressure to increase the viscosity of a product through reduction of water content or other means.

**Note 6.** For heading 2009, "juices, unfermented and not containing added spirit" means juices of an alcoholic strength by volume not exceeding 0.5 percent vol.

**Subheading notes.** "Homogenized vegetables" (2005.10) and "homogenized preparations" of fruit (2007.10) are finely homogenized preparations put up for retail sale as food for infants or young children or for dietetic purposes, in containers of not more than 250 g net; both subheadings take precedence over the others in their heading. For 2009.12, 2009.21, 2009.31, 2009.41, 2009.61 and 2009.71, "Brix value" is the direct Brix-hydrometer or refractometer reading at 20 °C.
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**Note 1.** For heading 2009: (a) "liter" in the rates for fruit juices means a liter of natural unconcentrated or of reconstituted fruit juice; (b) "reconstituted fruit juice" is the product obtained by mixing the imported concentrate with water to the average Brix value of the like natural juice, as found by the Secretary of the Treasury; (c) "Brix value" is the refractometric sucrose value, adjusted for added sweeteners and corrected for acid.

**Note 2.** The liters of reconstituted juice a concentrate yields are calculated on a volume basis to the nearest 0.5 degree of concentration; a juice with a degree of concentration under 1.5 is treated as natural unconcentrated juice.

**Note 3.** A mixture of fruit juices is treated, for its degree of concentration, as consisting wholly of the component juice with the lowest Brix value.

**Note 4.** Olives entered under subheadings 0711.20.18 and 2005.70.06 may not exceed 4,400 metric tons in aggregate in any calendar year.

**Note 5.** Peanut butter and paste entered under subheading 2008.11.05 may not exceed, per calendar year: Canada 14,500 t, Argentina 3,650 t, the countries listed in note 6 together 1,600 t, other countries 250 t. Products of Mexico are not included in this quota.

**Note 6.** Lists the countries and territories that share the 1,600-ton aggregate quantity in note 5.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 20: Preparations of Vegetables, Fruit, Nuts or Other Parts of Plants — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 20 Tariff Updates: Orange Juice, Canned Vegetables, Fruit & Juices Since 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 20 (processed fruit, vegetables, nuts and juices) since January 2025: base rates on all 285 lines, the end of the IEEPA duties, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs and the orange-juice exemptions, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). No Chapter 20 base rate changed between them; 16 new statistical lines split out certified-organic products at the same rates.

Everything that changed came on top of the base rate. The 2025 IEEPA duties (Canada +35%, Mexico +25%, Brazil +40%, the reciprocal tariff on everyone else) **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%** — except on the **29 lines on the exemption list**, which include orange juice, canned pineapple, mango and papaya products, coconut and palm hearts. China also pays its 2018–2019 Section 301 duties (up to **37.5%** in all) and Brazil a separate 25% (**37.5%** in all). **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt.**
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 20 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies and their exemption lists, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the China Section 301 Lists 3 and 4A, the phased Nicaragua Section 301 duty, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. Antidumping and countervailing duties are listed on the documents page, not here. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 20 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 269 Chapter 20 lines that exist in both editions carry the same General, FTA and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. The 16 new 10-digit statistical lines, most of them separating certified-organic products from existing lines (for example 2009.12.25.10 organic not-from-concentrate orange juice) at their parent line's rate. Revision 21 itself changed only Chapter 38 and a China exclusion note in Chapter 99.

changes.title: Nicaragua Section 301 duty: 10% from 2027, 15% from 2028
changes.detail: USTR set a phased duty on products of Nicaragua (9903.89.01): 0% in 2026, 10% from January 1, 2027 and 15% from January 1, 2028. It does not apply to goods that originate under CAFTA-DR and are entered under it (U.S. note 29). It comes on top of the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty on Nicaragua (9903.05.58).

changes.title: FDA lowers the minimum Brix for pasteurized orange juice
changes.detail: The standard of identity for pasteurized orange juice (21 CFR 146.140) now requires at least 10° Brix instead of 10.5°, and allows up to 15% by volume of mandarin (Citrus reticulata) or its hybrid juice. Imported juice sold as "pasteurized orange juice" must meet the standard. No tariff change.

changes.title: Antidumping orders on preserved mushrooms continued
changes.detail: After the fifth sunset review, Commerce continued the antidumping orders on certain preserved mushrooms (2003.10) from Chile, China, India and Indonesia, in place since 1998–1999. Separate orders on preserved mushrooms from France (January 2023) and the Netherlands, Poland and Spain (May 2023) also remain. These cash deposits are on top of the tariff; the rates on this site do not include them.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies — 29 Chapter 20 lines exempt
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84), on 256 of 285 Chapter 20 lines. The general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86) covers 29 lines — orange, lime and concentrated pineapple juice, canned pineapple, mango, papaya, banana, coconut, palm hearts and others — and note 52(c) exempts described açaí and coconut-water products. EU goods pay 10% in total and Japan, South Korea and Switzerland 12.5% in total where the base rate is lower. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil — orange juice exempt
changes.detail: 25% on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). The exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03) includes the same 20 Chapter 20 subheadings as the 2026 list, among them orange juice and orange pulp; açaí, coconut water and some citrus juices are exempt when they match the described article (9903.05.04). From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top for goods not on the lists.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs — 19 Chapter 20 subheadings exempt
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. The product exemption list (9903.03.03) included 19 Chapter 20 subheadings — orange, lime and concentrated pineapple juice, canned pineapple, mango, papaya, banana and coconut products among them. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: Brazil 40% IEEPA duty: more Chapter 20 goods exempted
changes.detail: Executive Order 14361 (signed November 20, 2025) widened the list of agricultural goods of Brazil exempt from the 40% duty (9903.01.77; exemption list 9903.01.81), for goods entered from November 13, 2025. In the final schedule the list names 24 Chapter 20 subheadings — the orange-juice lines exempt since August 2025 plus açaí, coconut water, mango, papaya, banana, pineapple and other tropical-fruit preparations. The duty ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Tropical fruit products and orange juice taken out of the reciprocal tariff
changes.detail: Executive Order 14360 added agricultural products to the reciprocal-tariff exemption list (U.S. note 2(v)(iii), 9903.01.32), for goods entered from 12:01 a.m. EST on November 13, 2025. For Chapter 20 it listed 19 subheadings — orange juice, lime and concentrated pineapple juice, canned pineapple, mango, papaya, banana, coconut and palm-heart preparations among them — plus açaí, coconut water and certain citrus juices by description. Other Chapter 20 goods stayed subject until all IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026.
changes.countries: All countries subject to the reciprocal tariff

changes.title: FDA revokes 11 unused canned fruit and vegetable standards
changes.detail: FDA revoked the standards of identity for 11 canned fruit and vegetable products no longer sold in the United States (direct final rule, effective date confirmed September 26, 2025). The standards for products still sold, such as canned tomatoes and fruit preserves, are unchanged.

changes.title: 40% IEEPA duty on products of Brazil — orange juice exempt
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 (signed July 30, 2025) added 40% on goods of Brazil from August 6, 2025, on top of the 10% reciprocal duty. Its annex exempted orange juice (2009.11.00, 2009.12.25, 2009.12.45) and orange pulp (2008.30.35) from the start. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 20 goods rose from **$15.22B in 2024 to $15.96B in 2025** (+4.9%), and have grown about 75% since 2020 ($9.15B). The two largest groups are prepared fruit and nuts (heading 2008, $4.96B) and juices (2009, $4.60B), followed by frozen vegetables (2004, $2.50B) and other preserved vegetables (2005, $2.17B).

Each big supplier has its own product. **Canada** ($2.83B) ships mostly heading 2004 — $1.74B, where frozen potato products such as French fries (2004.10) are $2.13B of the $2.50B heading. **Mexico** ($2.24B) leads in prepared fruit and nuts ($1.07B) and pickled vegetables. **Brazil** ($1.60B, +19%) is the largest juice supplier ($1.54B of heading 2009), much of it orange juice; frozen orange juice alone (2009.11) was $488M. Thailand, Vietnam and China supply canned and prepared fruit; Spain and Greece preserved vegetables and olives (heading 2005), Italy tomatoes.

USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico — 32% of 2025 imports — enter free. Orange juice, canned pineapple and most tropical-fruit preparations are on the Section 301 exemption list, which covers much of what Brazil and Thailand ship. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data.

seo.shortDescription: The total U.S. tariff on processed fruit, vegetables, nuts and juices by country and product group: base rate plus the 2026 Section 301 duty, with USMCA, EU and exemption-list rules applied.
keywords: HTS Chapter 20 tariff rates by country

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on processed fruit, vegetables and juices depends on **where they come from** as much as on what they are. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** that started July 24, 2026. **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico enter free**, **EU goods pay at least 10%**, Thailand, Vietnam, Türkiye and Peru add 12.5%, and **Brazil and China add up to 37.5%**. Orange juice, canned pineapple and the other lines on the exemption list pay only the base rate (China still adds its older Section 301 duty).

rule.label: From no extra duty (countries outside the 60 Section 301 economies, e.g. Ukraine, Kenya, Fiji) to +12.5%, or 10%/12.5% in total for the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan (9903.05.20–9903.05.83). No country exception list names a Chapter 20 line.

assumptions: Each total was computed by the official-measures calculator engine (the same data as the tariff calculator: measures.json, HTSUS 2026 Revision 21) for goods entered on 2026-10-11, priced on a $10,000 shipment and 1,000 units for per-unit rates.
Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.
Preferences: USMCA (S) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side; PE for Peru. GSP (A, A+) has lapsed and is not applied. Other preferences are not applied.
Conditional relief is not applied (it needs the importer's confirmation): 9903.05.04 (Section 301), 9903.05.87 (Section 301).
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.
The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; neither is applied.

The 29 lines on the Section 301 general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)) are priced with no 2026 Section 301 duty for every country. Açaí, coconut water and certain citrus juices are exempt only when they match the described article (note 52(c)); the matrix charges them, since that needs the importer's confirmation.

Antidumping and countervailing duties are not included: preserved mushrooms (2003.10) from Chile, China, France, India, Indonesia, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain; ripe olives (2005.70) from Spain; lemon juice (2009.31) from Brazil and South Africa. They are set per exporter by Commerce.

Tariff-rate quotas are shown as the separate lines the schedule uses: peanut butter within the quota (2008.11.05, Free) and over it (2008.11.15, 131.8%); olives, satsumas and peanuts have similar in-quota lines.
The rate is not the only gate: FDA must be able to verify canned-food process filings, juice HACCP and the importer's FSVP before the goods are released (see the documents page).
industryAreas.exemptionCheck: Read U.S. notes 20, 29, 50, 51 and 52 to Chapter 99 subchapter III in the 2026 Revision 21. The Section 301 general exemption list (note 52(b), 9903.05.86) names 20 Chapter 20 subheadings (29 ten-digit lines), and the Brazil list (note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03) the same 20; note 52(c) and note 50(a)(iii) add açaí (2008.99.21), certain citrus juice (2009.31.60), coconut water or açaí juice (2009.89.70) and coconut-water blends (2009.90.40) by description. No country exception list in note 52(j) and no Canada Section 338 list (note 51) names a Chapter 20 line. China List 3 (note 20, 9903.88.03) covers 231 lines and List 4A (9903.88.15) the other 54; no 9903.88.69 exclusion covers a Chapter 20 line.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 20: Preparations of Vegetables, Fruit, Nuts or Other Parts of Plants — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Juice, Canned & Preserved Foods: FDA Rules & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 20) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The FDA filings and rules for each HTS Chapter 20 line — food facility registration, prior notice, FSVP, low-acid and acidified canned-food process filing, juice HACCP — plus antidumping orders and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, the Section 301 exemption list, quotas, drawback.
keywords: FDA requirements for importing canned food
low acid canned food registration FCE SID

tariffEngineering.intro:
For processed fruit and vegetables, **FDA paperwork decides whether a shipment is released**. Every line needs a registered foreign facility, prior notice and an importer with a Foreign Supplier Verification Program. Canned low-acid and acidified foods need a registered canning establishment and a filed process for each product; juices must be made under juice HACCP.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: claim **USMCA** or another FTA, check whether the product is on the **Section 301 exemption list**, enter within a **tariff-rate quota**, or claim **drawback** on goods you re-export. Antidumping duties on mushrooms, olives and lemon juice are separate and are not modelled by the calculator.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The Section 301 duty — 10% of value for Canada or Mexico — plus any base rate (8% on French fries, 12.5% on canned tomatoes)
levers.appliesTo: All 285 lines, for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. It need not follow a prescribed format; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: Processed foods qualify under product-specific rules of origin, so fruit or vegetables grown outside North America may not make the finished product originating. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim another free trade agreement
levers.saves: The base rate: every dutiable line is Free for at least one FTA partner (Australia, Chile, Colombia, Israel, Korea, Morocco, Peru, CAFTA-DR …)
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable lines, for originating goods of the partner country (the special-rate column lists who qualifies)
levers.document: Proof of origin as the agreement requires (certification or declaration), kept on file and given to CBP on request.
levers.caveat: An FTA claim removes the base rate but not the 2026 Section 301 duty for that country (U.S. note 52(a)). Peanut butter over the quota (2008.11.15) is Free only for the partners listed on the line.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Check the Section 301 exemption list
levers.saves: The whole 2026 Section 301 duty (10%–12.5%, or 25% + 12.5% for Brazil) — the line pays only its base rate
levers.appliesTo: 29 lines: orange, lime and concentrated pineapple juice; canned pineapple; orange pulp; coconut; palm hearts; banana, mango and papaya preparations; pineapple jam; guava and mango purées; bamboo shoots; mangoes in vinegar; 2008.99.91
levers.document: Correct classification on the entry (the exemption follows the HTS subheading; CBP files it with 9903.05.86 / 9903.05.03).
levers.caveat: The list is by subheading, so a product classified one line over (for example pineapple juice of 2009.41 instead of 2009.49.40) pays the duty. China still pays its List 3 or 4A duty on these lines.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 50(a)(ii) and 52(b)

levers.title: Confirm a described exempt article (açaí, coconut water, certain citrus juice)
levers.saves: The 2026 Section 301 duty, and for Brazil also the 25% Brazil duty
levers.appliesTo: Açaí (2008.99.21), citrus juice other than orange, grapefruit, lime or lemon, concentrated (2009.31.60), coconut water or açaí juice (2009.89.70), coconut-water blends not from concentrate for retail sale (2009.90.40)
levers.document: Product specifications showing the goods are exactly the described article, entered under 9903.05.87 (and 9903.05.04 for Brazil).
levers.caveat: Other goods of the same subheading — other berries of 2008.99.21, other juices of 2009.89.70 — pay the duty.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 50(a)(iii) and 52(c)

levers.title: Enter within a tariff-rate quota
levers.saves: Peanut butter: Free instead of 131.8%. Olives, satsumas and peanuts: the lower in-quota rate
levers.appliesTo: Peanut butter and paste (2008.11.05 vs 2008.11.15) and the other in-quota lines (olives 2005.70.02/.06/.16/.91, satsumas 2008.30.42, peanuts 2008.11.02/.43/.46)
levers.document: Entry under the in-quota line while the quota for the country is open. The peanut-butter quota is allocated by country: Canada 14,500 t, Argentina 3,650 t, the countries in additional U.S. note 6 together 1,600 t, others 250 t.
levers.caveat: Products of Mexico are not counted in the peanut-butter quota; they enter under USMCA. Over-quota goods cannot claim drawback except unused-merchandise drawback (19 CFR 191.3(c)).

levers.title: Claim drawback on goods you export or destroy
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the ordinary customs duties paid, when the imported goods (or goods made from them) are exported or destroyed
levers.appliesTo: Any line, for importers who re-export — for example juice concentrate blended and shipped abroad
levers.document: A drawback claim filed with CBP with proof of import, use and export.
levers.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are never refunded, and over-quota agricultural goods only through unused-merchandise drawback (19 CFR 191.3). Confirm with CBP whether a given Chapter 99 duty is eligible before relying on it.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification — juice Brix and concentration, "prepared or preserved" vs. Chapter 7/8, exemption-list subheading — before the goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the classification decides the rate
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product, its ingredients and how it is processed and packed.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a different product or recipe may need its own.

rules.title: Food facility registration: the foreign plant that makes, packs or holds the food must be registered with FDA
Prior notice of every food shipment before it arrives
Foreign Supplier Verification Program (FSVP): the importer must verify each foreign supplier (for low-acid canned foods, that part 113 was followed)

Low-acid canned foods (pH above 4.6, shelf-stable in sealed containers): food canning establishment registration (Form FDA 2541) and a filed scheduled process per product (Forms 2541d/f/g); otherwise CBP refuses admission
Acidified foods (low-acid foods brought to pH 4.6 or below with acid, e.g. pickles, peppers, artichokes): establishment registration and process filing (Form FDA 2541e)
Juice HACCP: juice must be processed under a HACCP plan; the importer must hold the processor's plan, certificates or other proof, or the juice is denied entry

Standards of identity and juice labeling: canned fruit, fruit juices (incl. the 10° Brix pasteurized orange juice standard from August 19, 2026), jams, canned vegetables, peanut butter; percentage-juice declaration
Canned ripe olives: import inspection and minimum grade and size requirements (Section 8e)
Certified-organic lines: an NOP import certificate for each organic shipment

Antidumping / countervailing duty orders: cash deposits on preserved mushrooms (8 countries), ripe olives from Spain and lemon juice from Brazil and South Africa (Argentina: suspension agreement) — not modelled by the calculator

citations.label: 91 FR 48372: mushrooms from Chile, China, India, Indonesia continued (July 31, 2026)
88 FR 33096: mushrooms from the Netherlands, Poland, Spain (May 23, 2023)
89 FR 65324: ripe olives from Spain, AD and CVD continued (August 9, 2024)
88 FR 10088: lemon juice from Brazil and South Africa (February 16, 2023)
90 FR 8116: lemon juice from Argentina, suspension agreement (January 24, 2025)

groups.label: Pickles & vegetables in vinegar
groups.note: Pickles made by adding vinegar to low-acid vegetables are acidified foods; naturally acid foods and refrigerated products fall outside part 114.

groups.label: Tomatoes, prepared or preserved
groups.note: Tomato products with a finished pH below 4.7 are not low-acid foods (21 CFR 114.3(d)); those with a higher pH need LACF process filing.

groups.label: Mushrooms & truffles, preserved
groups.note: Canned mushrooms are usually low-acid foods. Agaricus mushrooms (2003.10) from Chile, China, France, India, Indonesia, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain are under antidumping orders.

groups.label: Frozen prepared vegetables, incl. French fries
groups.note: Frozen products are outside the canned-food rules (parts 113 and 114); the general FDA import rules apply.

groups.label: Other preserved vegetables & olives (not frozen)
groups.note: Which canned-food rule applies depends on the product's pH. Canned ripe olives (2005.70) also need USDA inspection, and ripe olives from Spain are under antidumping and countervailing orders.

groups.label: Fruit & peel preserved by sugar (candied, glacé)
Jams, jellies, marmalades & fruit purées
groups.note: Jams, jellies and preserves are excluded from the acidified-food rule (21 CFR 114.3(b)).

groups.label: Prepared fruit & nuts, incl. peanut butter & canned fruit
groups.note: Most canned fruit is naturally acid; low-acid items such as palm hearts or chestnuts need LACF or acidified process filing. Peanut butter has a standard of identity (21 CFR 164.150).

groups.label: Fruit & vegetable juices
groups.note: Every juice needs juice HACCP; low-acid juices such as coconut water or carrot juice packed shelf-stable also need LACF filing. Lemon juice (2009.31) from Brazil and South Africa is under antidumping orders.

seo.title: Orange Juice, Peanut Butter, Fries & Canned Food Tariffs FAQ (HTS Ch. 20) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about processed fruit, vegetable and juice tariffs: orange juice from Brazil, HS codes for juice, jam, pickles and peanut butter, French fries from Canada, coconut water, olives and canned mushrooms.
keywords: brazil orange juice us tariff exemption

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing processed fruit, vegetables, nuts and juices into the U.S. — tariffs by country, HS codes and FDA requirements. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico enter free — no base rate, no extra duty.

The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026. Since July 24, 2026 the extra duty is a Section 301 tariff: 10% in total for most EU goods, +10% or +12.5% for most other suppliers, +37.5% for Brazil and up to +37.5% for China.
29 lines — orange juice, canned pineapple, mango, papaya, banana, coconut and palm-heart products among them — are exempt from that duty for every country.
Antidumping duties on preserved mushrooms, Spanish ripe olives and lemon juice come on top of the tariff, and FDA canned-food and juice rules decide whether a shipment is released.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on orange juice?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on orange juice
faqs.answer: Only the base rate, for every country except China. Frozen concentrate (2009.11) is 7.85¢ per liter of reconstituted juice, not-from-concentrate orange juice (2009.12.25) 4.5¢ per liter. Orange juice is on the exemption list of the 2026 Section 301 tariff (U.S. note 52(b)), so no extra duty is added; USMCA and most FTA partners pay nothing at all. Orange juice from China still pays the 2018–2019 Section 301 duty (25% or 7.5%).

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on orange juice from Brazil?
searchedAs: brazil orange juice us tariff exemption
faqs.answer: Just the base rate: 7.85¢ per liter for frozen concentrate, 4.5¢ for not-from-concentrate. Brazilian orange juice and orange pulp are exempt from both Section 301 duties on Brazil — the 25% Brazil tariff (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)) and the 12.5% 2026 tariff (note 52(b)). They were also exempt from the 40% IEEPA duty of 2025, which ended February 24, 2026. Brazil shipped $1.54B of juices to the U.S. in 2025, $488M of it frozen orange juice.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for orange juice?
searchedAs: hs code for orange juice concentrate
faqs.answer: 2009.11 for frozen orange juice (concentrate), 2009.12 for orange juice not frozen with a Brix value up to 20 (2009.12.25 not-from-concentrate, 2009.12.45 other), and 2009.19 for other orange juice. The U.S. rates are per liter of single-strength juice, so concentrate is counted at the volume it makes once reconstituted (Chapter 20 additional U.S. notes 1–2).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for fruit juice?
searchedAs: hs code for fruit juice concentrate
faqs.answer: Heading 2009 covers unfermented fruit and vegetable juices: orange 2009.11–2009.19, grapefruit 2009.21–2009.29, other citrus 2009.31–2009.39, pineapple 2009.41–2009.49, tomato 2009.50, grape 2009.61–2009.69, apple 2009.71–2009.79 (Free), other single juices such as coconut water and cherry juice 2009.81–2009.89, and juice mixtures 2009.90. Juice with more than 0.5% alcohol is Chapter 22; juice drinks with added sugar or water are usually heading 2202.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on peanut butter, and what is its tariff code?
faqs.answer: Peanut butter and paste is 2008.11. Within the yearly quota it enters under 2008.11.05, Free; over the quota it is 2008.11.15 at 131.8%. The quota is set by country: Canada 14,500 t, Argentina 3,650 t, a group of listed countries 1,600 t together, all others 250 t. Mexico is outside the quota and enters free under USMCA. Section 301 duties for the country apply on top.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on French fries from Canada?
faqs.answer: Not if they qualify for USMCA. Frozen French fries are 2004.10.80, with an 8% base rate that USMCA makes Free, and USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt from the 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian products (9903.05.93). Fries that do not qualify pay 8% + 10%. From the EU (Belgium, the Netherlands) they pay 10% in total (9903.05.39). Canada shipped $1.74B of frozen prepared vegetables, mostly potato products, to the U.S. in 2025.

faqs.question: Is coconut water exempt from tariffs?
faqs.answer: Coconut water is 2009.89.70, with a base rate of 0.5¢ per liter. It is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariff when it is entered as the described article "coconut water or juice of açaí" (U.S. note 52(c), 9903.05.87), and blends of coconut water not from concentrate for retail sale (2009.90.40) have the same exemption. FDA juice HACCP applies, and shelf-stable packs of a low-acid juice also need canned-food process filing.

faqs.question: What is the tariff code and duty for tomato paste and canned tomatoes?
faqs.answer: Canned tomatoes, whole or in pieces, are 2002.10 (12.5%); tomato paste, purée and other tomato preparations are 2002.90.80 (11.6%), and tomato powder 2002.90.40 (11.6%). Ketchup and tomato sauces are Chapter 21, not here. From Italy and the rest of the EU the total stays 12.5% or 11.6%: the EU Section 301 rate only lifts lower rates to 10%.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for pickles?
faqs.answer: Pickles preserved in vinegar are heading 2001: cucumbers and gherkins 2001.10 (9.6%), and other vegetables, fruit and nuts in vinegar 2001.90 — capers 8%, artichokes 10.2%, onions 3.6%, peppers 8.1%. Vegetables preserved by brine or fermentation without vinegar, such as sauerkraut (2005.99.30, 4.8%) and kimchi, generally fall in heading 2005.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and duty for jam?
faqs.answer: Heading 2007. Most jams are 2007.99: strawberry 2.2%, lingonberry and raspberry 1.8%, apricot 3.5%, cherry 4.5%, peach 7%, pineapple 4%, other 5.6%. Citrus marmalade is 2007.91, and homogenized fruit preparations for infants (up to 250 g) are 2007.10. Pastes and purées of apple, strawberry or papaya run 12%–14%.

faqs.question: What tariffs apply to olives from Spain?
faqs.answer: Prepared olives are 2005.70, charged per kilogram of drained weight — for example 10.1¢/kg on canned pitted or sliced black (ripe) olives and 8.6¢/kg on pitted or stuffed green olives. As EU goods they pay at least 10% in total under the Section 301 action (9903.05.39). Ripe (black) olives from Spain also face antidumping and countervailing duties, continued in August 2024, which are not included in the rates shown here. Canned ripe olives must also pass USDA inspection (7 CFR 944.401).

faqs.question: Are there antidumping duties on canned mushrooms?
faqs.answer: Yes. Preserved Agaricus mushrooms (2003.10) from Chile, China, India and Indonesia have been under antidumping orders since 1998–1999 (continued again on July 31, 2026), and from France, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain since 2023. The tariff itself is 6¢/kg on drained weight + 8.5%, plus the Section 301 duty for the country.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on canned pineapple?
faqs.answer: Canned and otherwise prepared pineapple is 2008.20, at 0.35¢/kg, and it is on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list — so canned pineapple from Thailand, the Philippines or Indonesia pays only 0.35¢/kg. Pineapple juice is 2009.41 (Brix up to 20) or 2009.49; only the concentrated 2009.49.40 line (1¢/liter) is on the exemption list.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on açaí from Brazil?
faqs.answer: Prepared açaí is 2008.99.21, with a 4.5% base rate. Products described as "açaí" are exempt from both the 25% Brazil Section 301 tariff (9903.05.04) and the 12.5% 2026 tariff (9903.05.87), so Brazilian açaí pays 4.5%. Açaí juice (2009.89.70, 0.5¢/liter) has the same exemption.

faqs.question: How much processed fruit, vegetables and juice does the U.S. import?
faqs.answer: $15.96B of Chapter 20 goods in 2025, up 4.9% from 2024. Prepared fruit and nuts ($4.96B) and juices ($4.60B) are the largest groups. Canada ($2.83B), Mexico ($2.24B) and Brazil ($1.60B) are the top suppliers.
